question: How can I teach my teenage daughter modesty when Muslim influencers online promote different values?
asked: A mother says her teenage daughter is being influenced by the society around us, and even by Muslimahs on Snapchat and Instagram who claim to be preaching Islam and teaching morality, ethics and modest dressing, but who promote values and dress in a manner very different from what she is trying to instill in her daughter. How can she teach her daughter that this is not the ideal image of a Muslimah?
answer:
Now, the problem comes: we live in such a hypersensitive society that it is very difficult these days for any man to speak about how women should or should not dress without there being a huge backlash that this is something misogynistic, etc., etc. And it's a very difficult and sensitive topic, and I am hesitant to go down this route because of this. At the same time, we do have a responsibility to all men and women, to all of our youngsters, teenage men and teenage women, and boys and girls before that, that we teach them the values of Islam.

And by the way, the question is a mother asking for her daughter. Dear sister, realize I have sons and daughters. I'm worried for both of them. It's not just the daughters; it's also the sons as well. We are worried that overall we live at a time where fahishah has become the norm, where even those that are attempting to dress modestly, their versions of modesty are different sometimes than what Islam promotes.

And there is also a gray area; Islam itself allows for some gray area. So the issue of what type of hijab, and the issue of how the fabric is going to be, and what colors it can be: even the shariah does actually have an area where it is not explicit. The shariah does not say wear black. The shariah does not say cover yourself head to toe in a complete burqa or chador, even though there's nothing wrong with that. So I'm not saying that's wrong. But does the shariah require that you wear a black jilbab and a black hijab? It's not required. The way that, for example, we find it in Afghanistan or in Saudi, that they have the burqa coming straight down from the head, and it is not even from the shoulders, that is a version. There's nothing wrong with that; it is something that does protect the body. But how about a sister wearing a very loose shirt and very loose pants? Because again, the problem comes that even for brothers, we cannot have tight... If the brothers were to wear a speedo garment or tight jeans that is completely describing the 'awrah, we would say that is not allowed. So it's a two-way street, brothers and sisters.

Now, the sister is asking, how can we instill haya in our children? And I have to be honest with you: there is no easy way to do that. Wallahi, it is difficult, and I am struggling just as much as you are. I too have children in this society. We're all living in this society together, and we are inundated with images and with movies and with television that is preaching a very different message of morality and sexuality. And to compound that issue, we are also in a time frame where this is very, very sensitive to speak about, and it is very easy to make life difficult for those who say things in too blunt a manner. And this is something that is definitely very problematic for all of us. And we have to balance between our morality and teaching our morality in a wise manner, and our values, and making sure that we're allowed to preach our values without getting banned or shut down.

You know, in some governments, by the way... alhamdulillah, in America we have the First Amendment; it's not going to be the government. But in some lands, in some countries in the world, it is possible for you to face a legal battle, maybe even go to jail, for saying things about morality and about gender and about sexuality that society considers to be beyond... So we have to be very careful how we phrase these things, and move on. At the same time, no matter what society says, we have a responsibility; we have to answer to Allah on the Day of Judgment. And we have to raise our children in a manner that we have done our job.

So what I do advise, first and foremost: you and your spouse have to embody that morality and that haya and that decency in your own lives. This is the number one mechanism. You have to show what it means to be a Muslim.

Number two, the people you associate with should also have that same level of haya and modesty and hijab and hishmah that you are comfortable with. Birds of a feather flock together; we said this 20 minutes ago, I'm saying it again now. So your son and daughter need to see, via your own family friends, by the people you hang around, what it means to live an Islamic life. You have to understand that they will absorb these values in a way that they're going to see it, and not just read about it.

Number three, try your best to teach them via your speech. When they see something that is inappropriate, or they're watching movies or TV or whatnot (and obviously we don't want to open this door that they can watch whatever they want; you monitor what they're watching), but when they see something, or when something is inappropriate, you comment, and you teach them in a wise and gentle manner, not just in a harsh manner. Because, you know, when they become teenagers and you just say, "Oh, astaghfirullah, astaghfirullah," they're going to make fun of astaghfirullah. Even that astaghfirullah, you know, they will find it funny. And you explain to them, "Do you know why we don't like this type of stuff?" Speak to them like adults. You know, the time is gone when, as I was growing up, your parents said astaghfirullah and you took it as astaghfirullah. These days, as you know, our children don't even understand, and they make fun of our values. Well, the only way to get this across is to treat them like adults, like young men and women. Sit them down, explain to them the dangers of free-license sexuality, the dangers of nudity, the dangers of just, you know, what society has become.

And I do hope, inshallah, it is a goal of mine, one day to give a more academic class that people can benefit from. But it is something that requires some time to prepare. And frankly, it is better if our sisters were to take this. I always recommend sisters to take charge of this, because they know best how to preach and teach to other sisters. And also, as you know, we live in a gender-charged society where, if a man says anything about women and women's dress, it is interpreted in a manner that it should not be. Because at the end of the day, our Prophet ﷺ was a man. What are you going to do? Tell the Prophet ﷺ that he should not have taught women how to dress? I mean... but anyway, that is the society that we live in.

So I will speak generically, and I'll say that no doubt all of us are struggling with this issue. And I can recommend, as I said: number one, you embody these values yourselves. Number two, your family and friends. Number three, talk to them like adults. Speak to them about why this is inappropriate. Don't just frown and tsk and say "astaghfirullah" and "tawbah, tawbah." Explain to them. And if you have to do some research to explain, go ahead and do some research. There's a lot of good books and academic articles, even YouTube videos out there, that explain the dangers of the free-license sexuality that has come. And you know, parents, you're going to have to educate yourselves to educate your own children. And then, definitely, in the list of things you should do is lots of du'a to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala to protect your children, lots of du'a that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala makes your children righteous and pious.
